paper.title: MARSHAL: Incentivizing Multi-Agent Reasoning via Self-Play with Strategic LLMs

headline.label: average over all reasoning benchmarks tested

mechanisms.name: Turn-level advantage estimator
mechanisms.text: Every move gets its own reward and advantage, so a win or a blunder late in the game is credited to the turns that caused it, not smeared over the whole trajectory.

mechanisms.name: Agent-specific advantage normalization
mechanisms.text: Each seat's advantages are normalized against that seat's own results (separate_norm_for_selfplay), because moving first or second changes what a good outcome looks like.

findings.title: The game score is raw, so it can be read directly
findings.body: critic/score/mean is the average over trajectories of one player's summed turn rewards, before any normalization (agentic_pipeline.compute_data_metrics: "score 为env的reward，raw value"). The normalized one is critic/rewards/mean. A turn earns +0.05 for a valid answer, the last turn adds +1 for a win, −1 for a loss or +0.1 for a draw, and a forfeit is −11. polaris_pbs_notes.md calls this score config-normalized; it isn't.

findings.title: In the Midway runs, no game got past move 2
findings.body: 0.5B smoke: X answered in the wrong format on move 1 in every game (score −11). 4B scale-up and megatron runs, every step: X made a valid opening (~220 tokens), then O's first answer ran into the 1024-token cap (1027 tokens) before closing </answer>, so O forfeited. That is exactly the −5.475 score: (0.05 + (−11)) / 2. Steps at −2.713 are the same games with three X trajectories per O trajectory in the batch.
findings.source: env/TicTacToe/* per-step metrics in the three Midway logs

findings.title: Identical outcomes give no learning signal
findings.body: With mean normalization per seat, every X trajectory scored 0.05 and every O trajectory scored −11, so each normalized reward is 0 and so is every advantage. That is why actor/pg_loss is exactly 0 in 14 of the 20 scale-up steps; the other six sit near 0.01, driven by rounding-level reward differences (about 1e-12), not by game outcomes. The bring-up proved the plumbing; it didn't train the policy.

findings.title: 400 steps on Polaris: the score moved once outcomes varied
findings.body: Same 1024-token cap, but the score climbed from about −5.4 (through step ~200) to −1.26 by step 300 and held. Over the run X's tokens per game fell from ~1683 to ~313 while O's stayed near 1480, and the winner metric went from 0.875 (O won 7 in 8) to 0.0 (X won every game). Rough reading, assuming equal X and O trajectories: −1.26 fits about one game in four still ending in an O forfeit and the rest won outright by X. The TensorBoard folder would confirm it.
findings.source: milestones in polaris_pbs_notes.md; estimate is ours

findings.title: In Decrypto, the MARSHAL checkpoint plays like its base model
findings.body: 32 Decrypto games (2026-10-30), Decrypto's own settings for both models. Eve won 29 of 32 games, so the team side sits near a floor: MARSHAL as Alice + Bob survived 1 of 16, the same as base Qwen3-4B. As Eve, MARSHAL intercepted in 16 of 16 games against 13 of 16 for the base model, a gap within noise at this size. Both answered in Decrypto's format almost every time (retries under 0.03 per move), so MARSHAL's tag-based training format didn't get in the way. As Eve, both models ran into Decrypto's 1024-token thinking budget on about 80% of moves.

findings.title: Why the bring-up can't be compared with the paper
findings.body: The paper reports evaluation results (win rates against fixed opponents on held-out games, and benchmark accuracy inside multi-agent systems); the bring-up recorded training diagnostics at 1/8 of the paper's trajectories per step and 1/4 of its answer length. The Arena on this display does the evaluation part on a small scale: base Qwen3-4B and the published MARSHAL checkpoint against the same opponents MARSHAL evaluates with, under the paper's token limits.
